Android lets FaunaLapse switch the screen off only if you allow it once, on the next screen. FaunaLapse then becomes a "device admin app" with one right only: to lock the screen. The session goes on with the screen off.

Pack photo sessions for the computer

A computer copies one large file much faster than thousands of photos (over a USB cable up to 9 times faster, most for small photos). Pack puts each finished photo session into one zip file, in the same folder. The photos are not compressed, so this is quick: about 1 to 2 minutes for 5000 photos of 1280 px, and up to 1.5 minutes per GB for larger photos (memory cards are the slowest). Best with the phone on the charger. Packing goes on with the screen off or in another app (a notification shows it); if Android stops it anyway, tap Pack again: nothing is lost. FaunaLapse reads each zip back and checks every file before it deletes the session folder. On the computer, extract the zip (Windows: right click, Extract All) to get the session folder back. A session larger than 4 GB, or one packed with little free space, gets more zip files (_part2 and on): extract them all into the same folder. Video sessions stay as they are: their few large files copy fast.

resources.string: This is the app\'s own folder: Android deletes it when the app is uninstalled. Allow the storage permission to save in Documents/FaunaLapse instead.
The camera closes; the photos and videos so far are kept.
Square: %1$d %% of the short side of the camera view, %2$s. Only the square is saved, in photos and video; focus and exposure follow it. %3$s

Saved in the record of each session. The values stay for the next sessions until you change them.
• Set up by, habitat, camera height and distance to the target are named as in Camtrap DP, a data standard for camera traps, so the records can be shared in it later.
• Plant: or what else you observe. Sample ID: for other targets. Session ID: your own name for a recording plan, the same for all its sessions. Both IDs take letters and digits.
• Distance to target: from the camera to the flower. Where the phone tells the lens distance, the fixed focus fills it in; type a measured value to replace it, or empty the field to take the focus distance again.
• Add a field: your own fields, for example Observer, Weather or Air temperature: text, notes, a number, a date, a time, yes or no, or a choice from your own list. They stay until you remove them; the record lists them under "custom".
• Get location: the GPS stays on until the uncertainty reaches your goal (10 m unless you change it; at most 3 min), then it switches off. Use it outdoors, under open sky; without network the first position can take a few minutes. A tap on the values it filled in asks before they can be changed.
• Or type latitude and longitude from another GPS device, and its uncertainty if it shows one. Empty all three fields to remove the position.
From the fixed focus (%1$s). The lens distance differs between phones: check it with a ruler now and then.

Android\'s ID for FaunaLapse on this phone; nobody can change it. It starts each session folder name, so files from several phones never mix. A factory reset gives a new one, and so does a FaunaLapse version signed by someone else (for example a test version). FaunaLapse cannot read an ID that survives a factory reset: Android allows that only to phone makers\' apps. For a lasting name, write it on the phone and add it as your own field, for example Device ID.
Choice from a list that you write
At most %1$d characters. For longer text, add a Notes field.
Its value goes too. You can add the field again later.

Photos of the surroundings, to document the site. They are taken at full size with the phone\'s camera app. At Start they move into the session folder, in its own folder site_photos, apart from the time-lapse photos; the record lists them with the text in About them. Take them before Start: during a session the camera is busy. Tap a photo to see it larger or to delete it.

Coordinate system: WGS 84 (EPSG:4326), decimal degrees, as GPS devices and web maps use. Typed values must use it too.

How far the true position may be from these coordinates. Android\'s GPS gives a radius with a 68 % chance of holding the true position (Camtrap DP: coordinateUncertainty). A typed value should come from the device that measured the position.

Get location stops as soon as the uncertainty is this value or less, and switches the GPS off. If the goal is not reached, it searches at most 3 min and keeps the best position. A smaller goal can make the search longer; 0 m always searches the full 3 min. The record keeps the goal with the position.
Under %1$d m is often not reached: the search may then run the full %2$d min and keep the best position.
0 m: the search always runs the full %1$d min and keeps the best position.
Uncertainty goal: use a whole number from 0 to %1$d m.
No position: tap Get location, or type it from another GPS device.
From this phone\'s GPS, at %1$s%2$s. A tap on these values asks before they can be changed.
Position: write both latitude and longitude (the uncertainty is optional), or leave all three empty.
Latitude, longitude and uncertainty come from this phone\'s GPS. Change them only for a better position, for example from another GPS device: the record then says they were typed by hand.
The uncertainty is above the goal of %1$d m: try again under open sky if you need it smaller.
Searching for GPS satellites until the uncertainty is ± %1$d m or less; keep the phone under open sky. Time: %2$d s of at most %3$d s.
Searching for GPS satellites for the full time (goal 0 m); keep the phone under open sky. Time: %1$d s of %2$d s.
Satellites: signal from %1$d, %2$d used for the position.
Best so far: no position yet.
No GPS position in %1$d s. Try again outdoors, away from buildings and trees.

Location is off: turn it on, then tap Get location again. Turn it off again when the position is saved.
FaunaLapse needs the precise location permission to save where the phone is. Tap Get location again to allow it.
Location is on: Get location can use the GPS.
Location is still on: switch it off for the field, so no app uses the GPS. Android lets only you switch it.
Location is off. Switch it on for Get location, and off again afterwards.
Photos: one every %1$s s for %2$s s, then %3$s min off.
Photos: one every %1$s s, without breaks.
Video, %1$d frames per s: clips of %2$s min, then %3$s min off.
Video, %1$d frames per s: clips of %2$s min, one after the other.
Screen off by itself %1$d min after the last touch.
Time between photos in a burst. Default 2 s: a 3 s step caught about 90 % of insect visits (Edwards et al. 2015).
Default 60 s: longer than a typical visit (about 11 s).

Photos and video: the square is shrunk to this size when saved. Any multiple of 32 from 224 to 4096, for example 320, 640, 1024 or 1280: detectors and video encoders work in blocks of 16 or 32 pixels, so these sizes need no padding. Default 1280 px: the input size of many insect detectors. A square with fewer real pixels is never enlarged: it is saved at its own size, rounded down to a multiple of 32 (the aim screen shows both). Old phones may save video smaller if their video encoder cannot take the size.
One video file per clip. Default 5 min.

Default 5: enough to follow insects from frame to frame on a computer. Use 10 or 15 for fast flying insects. Fewer frames give smaller files, but not in proportion: on a test phone, 5 frames per s took about 55 % of the storage of 15, and 10 about 80 %.
Default 5 min: the camera rests about 83 % of the time with 60 s photo bursts, and half of the time with 5 min clips. It is switched off when the break is longer than 30 s. 0 = no break.
Default 1 h, a usual observation period. Up to 720 h (30 days) without a break at night, for example under the midnight sun.

Clock times, for example 06:00-08:00, 17:00-20:00. A window may cross midnight (22:00-04:00), and 00:00-24:00 records all day (for example under the midnight sun). Default 05:00-21:00: early morning and evening visits count (Toivonen and Humberg 2026).
Default 1. Counted from the first window that is not over yet: a phone started in the evening records from the next morning. For more days, keep the phone on a power supply.

The camera stays off until the battery is 3 °C cooler. Default 45 °C: phones still work, but most stop charging near 45 °C and the battery wears fast above it. At most 50 °C. The session also stops cleanly when the battery falls to 15 % without charging, or when the storage is nearly full.

During a session, if Screen off is forgotten: FaunaLapse switches the screen off this many minutes after the last touch (a screen left on uses energy and warms the phone). 1 to 10 min, or 0 for never. Default 3 min: time to watch the first photos arrive. Not during a pause. Needs the Screen off right (the first tap on Screen off asks for it). The power button wakes the screen; a double tap works only on some phones.
Screen off is not allowed yet (the first tap on Screen off during a session asks): until then the phone\'s own screen timeout switches the screen off (now %1$s).
Never: the screen goes off with Screen off, the power button or the phone\'s own screen timeout (now %1$s).
On: %1$s. For the field, turn on airplane mode (flight mode) and keep Wi-Fi and Bluetooth off: radios use energy.
Location is on: other apps may use GPS. Turn it off for the field (after Get location).
Stay awake is on (in Developer options): while the phone charges, also from a power bank, its own screen timeout never switches the screen off. Turn it off for the field.
Battery limits apply to FaunaLapse: some phones then stop long sessions. In the settings, tap Battery (or App battery usage, Battery saver) and choose Unrestricted (or No restrictions).
Battery limits apply to FaunaLapse: some phones then stop long sessions. In the list, show all apps, tap FaunaLapse and choose Don\'t optimize.
FaunaLapse is restricted in the background: the phone may stop a session.
Airplane mode (flight mode) on; Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, location and Stay awake off; no battery limits for FaunaLapse: ready for the field.
A phone used only as a camera

A phone that does nothing else saves energy and is less likely to stop the app in the field:
• Reset it to factory settings; add no Google account and no SIM card.
• Turn off automatic app and system updates.
• Uninstall the apps you do not need, or disable them (in the phone's settings, under Apps).
• Set the clock, then turn on airplane mode (flight mode): without network the clock is not corrected, and the session record uses it.
• Some phones stop apps in the background with their own battery manager. Huawei: allow FaunaLapse to start and run in the background by hand (Battery, App launch). Xiaomi: set its battery saver to No restrictions. Samsung: add it to Never sleeping apps.
• Run a test session with the screen off before the field day.
After Start, tap Screen off on the status card (or press the power button gently): the session goes on with the screen off.

Camera2: the camera zooms onto the square in hardware, so a small square keeps its real detail.
Camera2: the camera can zoom only towards the middle, so a square near the middle keeps more detail.
In the middle (tap Middle), this phone can zoom onto the square: %1$d px.
Camera1: no hardware zoom, so the square has only its share of the stream\'s pixels.

Session paused: nothing is recorded. The session ends at %1$s.
The session went on by itself.
Lens position: %1$d of 100, from near to far (this phone does not tell the distance).
Auto: the camera focuses on the square at the start of each burst, then the lens stays. In a dense flower patch it may focus on another flower; Fixed avoids this.
Auto: the camera focuses on the square at the start of each clip, then the lens stays. In a dense flower patch it may focus on another flower; Fixed avoids this.

Fixed (default, starts at about 20 cm, a usual distance from phone to flower): the lens stays at this distance for the whole session and never focuses by itself, so bursts start faster, and wind, a passing insect or another flower cannot pull the focus away. Tap Focus again to focus once and fix the focus there, then adjust with the slider while you watch the view. Keep the phone where it is.

This phone cannot fix the focus: it focuses automatically on the square at the start of each burst or clip. In a dense flower patch, make the square cover mostly the target flower, so the camera focuses on it.
Focus: automatic at the start of each burst or clip.
Focus: fixed at %1$s; check it on the aim screen.
Focus: fixed at one lens position, set on the aim screen.
Focus: fixed at %1$s if this phone allows it; Aim the camera checks it.
Focus: automatic at the start of each burst or clip, because this phone cannot fix the focus.
Touch inside the square to move it.

Move the square onto the flower: put a finger inside it (or on its edge) and drag. A touch elsewhere does not move it. To make it larger or smaller, pinch with two fingers anywhere on the camera view, or use the slider; Middle puts it back in the middle. The small triangle marks the top of the saved photos and videos: it moves to the side when you hold the phone sideways, and stays at the top while the phone is upright or lies flat. Fix the phone in its place, then tap Start session here: the session uses this position.

For the developers, only in this test build: these tests measure what the back camera of a phone model can do, so FaunaLapse can be made to work well on it. Sessions do not need them.

One test photo: checks that the camera works with the screen off. It opens the camera with the older camera interface, waits 5 s for the exposure, focuses once, takes one full photo and closes.

Speed test (about 3 minutes): how fast full photos can follow each other (both camera interfaces, 4 photo sizes), how fast preview frames can be saved, and which video sizes and frame rates record. On a computer, tools/phase0_speed_report.py sums up the results.
